analysis.one_liner: Lets states — not the EPA — decide which large livestock feedlots must get water-pollution permits.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in December 2000 with no cosponsors and referred to committee, where it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the Clean Water Act, large animal feeding operations (feedlots) can be classified as 'concentrated animal feeding operations,' which requires them to get a federal pollution discharge permit. This bill would change the law so that each state, rather than the federal government, has the final say on which feedlots count — using factors like herd size, discharge volume, and site conditions. The bill was introduced in the final month of the 106th Congress, sent to the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Large livestock operations — big cattle, hog, and poultry feedlots — gain if the bill passes, because state-level classification standards could be looser than federal ones, keeping more operations out of the permitting system. States that prefer local control over feedlot rules also gain authority.

how_it_helps.text: Gives states final authority over which animal feeding operations are classified as concentrated feeding operations needing NPDES discharge permits, with state-set factors like animal units and discharge volume [S2][S3].
The state guidelines would weigh site-specific factors, which supporters would argue fits regulation to local conditions rather than applying uniform federal thresholds [S3].

analysis.who_pays: People living near feedlots and downstream water users bear the cost if the bill passes: state-by-state classification could exempt feedlots that federal rules would cover, allowing more manure and runoff into rivers, lakes, and drinking-water sources. Weakened federal oversight also removes a uniform national floor for water quality.

drawbacks.text: Turning classification over to states invites weaker standards in states with large agricultural industries, since the state would be the only check on which feedlots need permits [S3].
The bill contains no minimum federal criteria that state guidelines must meet, so a state could set factors that exempt most operations from permitting [S3].
Feedlot runoff is a major source of nutrient pollution in waterways; narrower classification means fewer operations monitored or required to control discharges [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is local flexibility — states could tailor feedlot classification to site conditions. But the bill removes the federal backstop entirely, with no minimum standards, in an area where weak state enforcement is a known risk. Because it affects water quality for people downstream of feedlots, the cost to the public likely outweighs the administrative convenience to states and operators.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee in its final month and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Nick Smith of Michigan introduced the bill on December 4, 2000, in the final month of the 106th Congress [S1].
It was referred to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure the same day, and no further action was taken [S5].
The Congress ended on January 3, 2001, so the bill died in committee without ever reaching the floor [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The federal permitting status quo stayed intact: large feedlots remained subject to federal classification rules, and downstream water users are better off than they would have been under the bill. The narrow winner of the bill's failure is anyone who benefits from continued federal oversight of feedlot pollution.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Downstream water users; federal oversight survived

for.name: Rep. Nick Smith
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to give states final authority over concentrated animal feeding operation classification.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by a single Republican with no cosponsors and never drew a vote, so no partisan pattern in support or opposition can be measured.

industries.note: The bill would let states set their own standards for which feedlots count as concentrated animal feeding operations, potentially keeping more large operations out of the federal pollution-permit system. That shifts the cost of manure and runoff onto downstream communities and water users.

States would gain final authority over feedlot classification, giving them flexibility to fit rules to local conditions. Whether that serves the public depends on each state's willingness to regulate agricultural polluters.
